blocks.text: Model introduction

“Good morning. My name is Dr ____. I understand you are considering injectable contraception. I would like to ask about your medical history, menstrual cycle, pregnancy plans and current medicines. I will then explain the available injections, how often they are given, their benefits and possible side effects, including changes in bleeding and the time it may take for fertility to return after stopping. Is that alright?”
Establish privacy, obtain consent and encourage questions. The patient must be free to choose another suitable method or discontinue injectable contraception.
Use the mnemonic INJECT.

blocks.text: Routine pelvic examination and laboratory tests are not required before every injection in an otherwise eligible patient. Measure blood pressure when clinically indicated, particularly when assessing cardiovascular risk or considering alternative methods.
A. Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA)

items.text: Commonly known as Depo-Provera.
Standard intramuscular formulation: 150 mg.
Typically administered every 13 weeks.
A subcutaneous formulation, DMPA-SC 104 mg, is also available and is generally administered every 12–14 weeks, according to product instructions.

blocks.text: B. Norethisterone enanthate (NET-EN)

items.text: Progestogen-only injectable contraception.
Common dose: 200 mg intramuscularly.
Typically repeated every eight weeks.
Availability varies by country.

blocks.text: C. DMPA-SC self-injection

items.text: A subcutaneous DMPA formulation supplied in a prefilled device in some settings.
May be self-administered after appropriate training where permitted.
Follow the exact product's storage, administration and repeat-injection instructions.

blocks.text: OSCE distinction: DMPA is generally repeated every 13 weeks, whereas NET-EN is generally repeated every eight weeks. Do not confuse the two schedules.

blocks.title: Injectable progestogens prevent pregnancy primarily through:

items.text: Suppression of ovulation: inhibit the hormonal events needed for the release of an ovum.
Thickening of cervical mucus: reduce sperm penetration through the cervix.
Endometrial changes: alter the endometrium.

blocks.text: DMPA provides prolonged contraceptive action because the medication is released gradually from the injection depot.
It is not an abortifacient and does not terminate an established pregnancy.
Injectable contraception is highly effective when injections are received on schedule.

items.text: No daily pill to remember.
Discreet administration.
No oestrogen.
Generally compatible with breastfeeding, subject to postpartum guidance.
May reduce menstrual bleeding over time.
Amenorrhoea is common with continued DMPA use.
May reduce dysmenorrhoea in some women.
DMPA effectiveness is generally not reduced by the enzyme-inducing medicines that compromise many pills and implants.

blocks.text: A disadvantage is that, once an injection has been given, its effects cannot be immediately reversed. If a patient develops troublesome adverse effects, the medication cannot simply be removed in the way an implant can.
Injectables do not protect against sexually transmitted infections. Offer condoms when STI protection is needed.
This is one of the most important counselling topics.

blocks.text: Explain that bleeding often becomes lighter or stops with continued DMPA use. However, the pattern is not fully predictable.
Persistent, heavy or painful bleeding should be assessed for pregnancy, infection and other causes when clinically indicated.
Some users experience weight gain, but the amount varies. Discuss this possibility without suggesting that every patient will gain weight.
This is a major examination point.

After the last DMPA injection, ovulation may take several months to resume, and conception can be delayed beyond a year in some patients. The delay varies between individuals and is not the same as permanent infertility.
If a woman hopes to become pregnant soon, discuss whether another reversible method better fits her timeline.
DMPA is associated with a reduction in bone mineral density during use. Recovery generally occurs after discontinuation, although the degree and time course vary.

blocks.text: Do not treat every condition as an absolute contraindication. Use the current WHO Medical Eligibility Criteria or applicable national guidance, taking the particular injectable and patient's circumstances into account.
Ask about the last menstrual period, recent unprotected intercourse and current contraceptive use.
Pregnancy should be reasonably excluded before routine initiation. A negative urine pregnancy test does not necessarily exclude conception from very recent intercourse.
If pregnancy cannot be excluded with certainty, follow an appropriate quick-start protocol where permitted, with follow-up pregnancy testing. The approach differs for injectables and IUDs.

content_groups.group_title: Step 2 — Explain the timing of initiation

blocks.text: For DMPA, the first injection can generally be given within the first seven days after menstrual bleeding begins without additional contraception.
If started later, backup contraception is generally required for seven days if pregnancy has been reasonably excluded.
Postpartum initiation and switching from another method require separate consideration of timing, pregnancy risk and existing contraceptive coverage.

blocks.text: The standard DMPA intramuscular formulation is administered by a trained clinician using the manufacturer's instructions. DMPA-SC may be self-administered after appropriate training where permitted.

Under CDC guidance, a repeat DMPA injection may be given up to 15 weeks after the previous injection without additional contraceptive protection.

blocks.text: Some national protocols use different grace periods. In an examination, state which guideline you are following and apply it consistently.

NET-EN is generally repeated every eight weeks. Its allowable delay and management of late injections should follow the relevant product information and local protocol; do not automatically apply the DMPA grace period to NET-EN.
Exam tip: always establish the exact injectable, the date of the last dose and the timing of recent unprotected intercourse before deciding whether backup or emergency contraception is needed.

content_groups.group_title: C. Women with hypertension or migraine

blocks.text: Because DMPA contains no oestrogen, it may be an alternative when combined hormonal contraception is unsuitable. However, severe hypertension, vascular disease and other comorbidities require individual assessment rather than automatic prescribing.

DMPA is generally not compromised by enzyme-inducing antiepileptics in the same way as the implant or oral hormonal methods. Check the current interaction guidance for the particular drug and formulation.

content_groups.group_title: E. Women who want pregnancy soon

blocks.text: Explain the possibility of delayed return to ovulation after DMPA. A pill, implant or IUD may be more suitable if rapid return to fertility is a priority, although fertility return varies between individuals and methods.

content_groups.group_title: Scenario A: Irregular bleeding after DMPA

blocks.text: History
Ask about bleeding duration, amount, pain, pregnancy possibility, injection dates, STI risk and symptoms suggesting another cause.
Management

items.text: Assess severity and haemodynamic stability if bleeding is heavy.
Consider pregnancy testing and investigations for infection or other pathology.
Reassure the patient if bleeding is consistent with expected side effects and there are no concerning features.
Consider short-term treatment under current guidance if the bleeding is troublesome.
Offer an alternative contraceptive method or discontinuation if she prefers.
Establish the amount and timing of weight change.
Review diet, activity and other possible causes.
Discuss the possibility of an association with DMPA without assuming causation.
Consider alternatives if weight change is unacceptable to the patient.

content_groups.group_title: Scenario C: A woman wants pregnancy after stopping DMPA

items.text: Explain that delayed ovulation is expected in some users.
Reassure her that this does not automatically indicate infertility.

subsections.subsection_title: 13. Common examiner questions and model answers

blocks.text: Q1. What is the standard repeat interval for DMPA?
DMPA intramuscular 150 mg is generally repeated every 13 weeks.
Q2. How does NET-EN differ from DMPA?
NET-EN is commonly given every eight weeks, whereas DMPA is generally given every 13 weeks.
Q3. Does DMPA cause permanent infertility?
No. It may delay the return of ovulation and conception after the last injection, but this is not the same as permanent infertility.
Q4. Why is bone health discussed with DMPA?
DMPA can reduce bone mineral density during use. The clinician should assess individual risk factors and discuss the benefits and risks of continued use.
Q5. What is the most important adverse effect to discuss?
Menstrual changes, including irregular bleeding and possible amenorrhoea, are essential counselling points. Delayed return to fertility is also particularly important.
Q6. Does DMPA protect against STIs?
No. Condoms are needed for STI risk reduction.
Q7. What would you advise a woman who wants pregnancy in three months?
I would explain that DMPA may delay return to ovulation and conception for several months or longer after the last injection. I would discuss alternatives that better match her reproductive timeline.
Q8. Can a woman breastfeed while using DMPA?
DMPA is generally compatible with breastfeeding, but the timing of initiation should follow applicable postpartum guidance and individual eligibility assessment.
